label: The Goths
pitch:
No Germanic people did more to end the ancient world. Remembering an origin across the Baltic in the island of Scandza, the Goths moved to the Black Sea, split into Visigoths and Ostrogoths, and then did the unthinkable: at the Battle of Adrianople in 378 they killed an emperor and destroyed his army, and in 410 Alaric Sacks Rome itself — the first time the city had fallen in eight hundred years.

They were also the most cultured of the barbarians. Ulfilas Translates the Gothic Bible into a brand-new alphabet, Theodoric the Great Conquers Italy and ruled it as a Roman philosopher-king from Ravenna, and Gothic law codes preserved Roman jurisprudence. Their story runs from the Scandza legend to Justinian's twenty-year war that finally erased Ostrogothic Italy in 554.

spans.label: The Gothic Migration South
spans.description: Gothic peoples moved from the Vistula basin to the Black Sea steppe, leaving the Wielbark culture and forming the Chernyakhov culture.

spans.label: The Gothic Raids on Rome
spans.description: Gothic sea and land raids devastated the Balkans and Asia Minor and killed the emperor Decius before Aurelian stabilized the frontier.

spans.label: Tervingi and Greuthungi Era
spans.description: The two main Gothic confederacies developed distinct identities on either side of the Dniester, the Tervingi under their reiks and the Greuthungi under Ermanaric's vast domain.

spans.label: The Gothic War of 376–382
spans.description: Driven across the Danube by the Huns, the Goths revolted, destroyed an imperial army at Adrianople, and won a treaty as armed federates inside the empire.

spans.label: The Visigothic Kingdom
spans.description: After sacking Rome the Visigoths settled in Aquitaine and then Hispania, building a kingdom centered on Toulouse and later Toledo.

spans.label: Ostrogothic Italy
spans.description: Theodoric the Great and his successors ruled Italy as a Gothic-Roman state from Ravenna, preserving the Senate, law, and classical culture.

spans.label: Justinian's Gothic War
spans.description: The Eastern Empire's twenty-year reconquest of Italy destroyed the Ostrogothic kingdom and devastated the peninsula.

events.label: Jordanes' Scandza Origin Legend
events.description: The only book-length account of Gothic origins is the Getica, written in Constantinople around 551 CE by a man named Jordanes — a summary, made partly from memory, of an earlier lost history written to flatter Gothic kings. It is the essential, deeply unreliable spine of everything we think we know about early Gothic history.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Jordanes says he produced the Getica in three days, working from memory of Cassiodorus's twelve-volume original, which he claims to have borrowed only briefly. The original Cassiodorus history is now completely lost, so there is no way to check how faithfully Jordanes summarized it. Jordanes describes himself as of Gothic descent but writes in Latin, making him one of the very few people of Gothic background to leave any writing at all.

events.label: The Wielbark Culture
events.description: The Wielbark culture — named after a site near modern Malbork in northern Poland — is the archaeological fingerprint scholars associate with early Gothic communities along the Vistula River, from roughly the first century through the Gothic migration south.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The Wielbark culture is notable for replacing the preceding Oksywie culture in the lower Vistula region, and its spread southeastward tracks the route the Gothic migration legend describes. The culture's distinctive mix of cremation and inhumation burials in the same cemetery is rare for Iron Age northern Europe. Wielbark sites show a striking near-absence of weapons in graves — unusual for a warrior society — suggesting a belief system that separated martial identity from the afterlife.

events.label: Wielbark Burial Rites
events.description: Wielbark cemeteries mix cremation and laid-out inhumation burials side by side, and they stand out sharply from neighboring cultures by burying almost no weapons — even in the graves of wealthy individuals — while lavishing the dead with amber beads, silver brooches, and imported Roman goods.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The near-total absence of weapons in Wielbark graves puzzles archaeologists because weapon burial was standard practice in the surrounding Germanic and Baltic Iron Age world. Baltic amber found in Wielbark graves was a high-value export commodity: Roman writers prized it so heavily that a single amber ornament could be worth more than a healthy slave in Rome's markets. Roman coins and bronze vessels appear in Wielbark graves despite the communities being several weeks' travel from the nearest Roman province.

events.label: Gothiscandza: The First Gothic Homeland
events.description: In the Gothic origin legend recorded by Jordanes, Gothiscandza — roughly "the Gothic coast" — was the name the migrants gave to their landing point on the southern Baltic shore after sailing south from Scandza (almost certainly Scandinavia), the starting line of the whole Gothic story.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Jordanes names a king called Berig as leading the founding fleet of three ships, a suspiciously round number common to origin myths. The legend explains the origin of the Gepids — a closely related people who were real historical actors — by claiming their ship fell behind, earning them the mocking nickname meaning "the sluggards." Most scholars locate Gothiscandza somewhere along the coast of what is now northern Poland, though no site has been confirmed archaeologically.

events.label: Baltic Amber Trade Routes
events.description: Gothic communities settled along the Vistula sat astride the Amber Road — the ancient trade corridor that carried fossilized Baltic tree resin south to Roman Mediterranean markets for centuries — making them prosperous participants in long-distance commerce rather than isolated forest peoples.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Baltic amber (succinite) washing up on North Sea and Baltic beaches is found in burial sites as far away as ancient Egypt, showing the trade route predates Rome by well over a thousand years. Roman demand was so intense that Emperor Nero reportedly sent an expedition specifically to the Baltic coast to source amber supplies for gladiatorial games. The trade brought not just coins but actual Roman luxury goods — glass, wine, bronze vessels — deep into the Baltic interior, meaning Gothic villagers had been physically handling pieces of the empire long before they ever attacked it.

events.label: The Goths Migrate to the Black Sea
events.description: By the early-to-mid third century CE, peoples the Roman world was labeling Goths had completed a multigenerational southward migration from the Vistula basin to the Pontic steppe (the grasslands north of the Black Sea), arriving at the edge of the Roman frontier with appetite and momentum.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Roman sources first specifically mention Goths in the 3rd century AD, placing them north of the lower Danube in what is now Ukraine, Moldova, and Romania. The driving engine of the migration was almost certainly land pressure: Baltic-zone farming with iron tools and short growing seasons left little room for surplus population, and the Roman world's wealth — already physically present in Gothic villages via the amber trade — pointed south like a compass needle. The archaeological Chernyakhov culture, which flourished across the Black Sea steppe in the 3rd and 4th centuries, is the material trace of the Goths in their new homeland.

events.label: Gothic Absorption of Oksywie Communities
events.description: As Wielbark-associated groups moved southward along the Vistula in the second and third centuries, they absorbed or displaced the earlier Oksywie culture — a neighboring Iron Age society — expanding the zone of Wielbark material culture in the process.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The Oksywie culture (named for a site near modern Gdynia) preceded the Wielbark in the lower Vistula region and shared the broader Germanic cultural sphere. The transition between them is not obviously violent in the archaeological record — graves shift style rather than showing destruction layers — suggesting assimilation rather than outright conquest. Modern archaeologists debate whether the Wielbark expansion represents one ethnic group displacing another or a change in burial fashion spreading through an existing population.

events.label: The Chernyakhov Culture
events.description: The Chernyakhov culture is the archaeological fingerprint left by the Goths and their neighbors across modern Ukraine, Romania, and Moldova — a dense, multi-ethnic zone of settlements, workshops, and trade goods that overturns every stereotype of Gothic barbarism.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The culture is named after a site in Ukraine, and it flourished from the 2nd through the 5th centuries AD across a massive swath of Eastern Europe. Scholars once hotly debated whether it represented the Goths at all, but advances in methodology have made the connection, in the words of historians Matthews and Heather, "irresistible." The population was genuinely mixed — Gothic, Geto-Dacian, and Sarmatian peoples living and working side by side — which is why "Chernyakhov culture" describes an economic zone, not a single ethnicity.

events.label: Chernyakhov Wheel-Thrown Pottery
events.description: Chernyakhov settlements produced wheel-thrown, kiln-fired pottery at a quality local regions had never seen before — evidence not of nomadic raiders but of full craft specialization, with dedicated potters, iron smelters, bronze smiths, and bone-comb makers running a working market economy.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Hand-built pottery can be made by any village household; wheel-thrown, kiln-fired pottery at scale requires specialists who make only pots, a market to sell them in, and a society organized enough to feed people who don't grow their own food. Chernyakhov workshops also turned out silver belt fittings and brooches — the prestige accessories of a culture that wanted to look wealthy, because it was. The culture's span ran from the 2nd to the 5th century AD, and at its height stretched across Ukraine, Romania, and Moldova.

events.label: Goths at the Roman Frontier Markets
events.description: Regular treaty markets along the Danube frontier let Gothic groups swap grain, hides, and slaves for Roman wine, olive oil, glassware, and silver coin — the flow of prestige goods that turned Gothic chiefs into serious warlords.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The exchange was structured: Rome set up designated border markets (called fora) to control and tax the flow. Roman amphora jars — the tall clay containers that shipped wine and olive oil in bulk — turn up in Chernyakhov sites far into the Gothic interior, showing goods moved well beyond the frontier zone itself. The wealth didn't just enrich individuals; it was reinvested in armed followings, because in this world a chief's loyal retinue stayed loyal exactly as long as the gold kept coming.

events.label: First Gothic Raids Across the Danube
events.description: Around 238 CE, Gothic groups crossed the lower Danube into the Roman province of Moesia (roughly modern Bulgaria and Serbia), exploiting the political chaos after Emperor Maximinus Thrax was murdered — and discovered that raiding the empire worked.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The timing was everything: the empire was entering what historians call the Crisis of the Third Century, a fifty-year stretch of civil wars, plague, and near-collapse during which emperors rose and fell at a terrifying pace. A successful first raid came home loaded with silver, slaves, and prestige, and in a world where a war-leader's followers stayed loyal only as long as he kept delivering, one successful raid made the next raid nearly inevitable. The Gothic Wars that followed would continue, on and off, for over three centuries.

events.label: Emperor Decius' Danube Campaigns
events.description: Decius, a Balkan-born soldier who had seized the throne in 249, personally led Roman armies into the Balkans to drive back Gothic raiders — the kind of hands-on frontier soldiering that had made him emperor in the first place.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Decius's full name was Gaius Messius Quintus Trajanus Decius — the 'Trajanus' was a deliberate nod to the conquering emperor Trajan, a piece of political branding meant to project strength. He reigned less than two years before dying at Abritus, the shortest reign of any emperor who tried and failed to stabilize the Danube frontier in this period.

events.label: Battle of Abritus — Decius Killed
events.description: At Abritus in Moesia (northeastern Bulgaria) in 251 CE, a Gothic army under Cniva lured a Roman force onto marshy ground and destroyed it, killing Emperor Decius and his son — the first sitting Roman emperor ever killed in battle against a foreign enemy.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The Roman historian Ammianus Marcellinus ranked Abritus alongside the catastrophes of Teutoburg Forest (9 CE) and the later Battle of Adrianople (378 CE) as one of Rome's worst military disasters. The battle was also known in ancient sources as the Battle of Forum Terebronii. Some Roman accounts hint at treachery within Roman ranks on the day, which would make the defeat partly an inside job rather than a clean Gothic triumph.

events.label: Cniva and the Gothic Siege of Philippopolis
events.description: The Gothic king Cniva led the first Gothic campaign we can follow in detail, besieging and sacking the major Roman city of Philippopolis (modern Plovdiv, Bulgaria) around 250 CE and hauling off vast plunder and thousands of captives.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: After destroying the army of Emperor Decius at Abritus in 251, Cniva negotiated from a position of total strength: the new emperor Trebonianus Gallus actually paid Cniva tribute and let him withdraw with all his spoils unmolested, a humiliation Rome had rarely swallowed. Cniva is the first Gothic individual whose campaigns can be reconstructed, yet everything we know about him comes from Roman writers describing the man who beat them.

events.label: Gothic Threat to Thessalonica
events.description: Gothic raiders pressed deep into Macedonia, menacing the major city of Thessalonica and demonstrating the empire's inability to hold the Balkan interior.

events.label: Gothic Sea-Raids on the Aegean
events.description: Through the 250s and 260s CE, Gothic war-leaders assembled fleets using Greek coastal populations and Black Sea shipbuilding skills, then sent them through the Bosphorus and Dardanelles into the Aegean — the first time a Germanic people went to war by sea.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The Goths had zero seafaring tradition of their own; they got their ships by controlling the Greek-descended coastal cities along the Black Sea's northern shore, whose populations knew how to build and sail vessels. This was two full centuries before the Vandals built a Mediterranean navy — making the Goths the pioneers of Germanic naval warfare, a fact that rarely gets the credit it deserves.

events.label: Gothic Sack of Athens
events.description: Around 267 CE, seaborne Germanic raiders sacked Athens — the intellectual and symbolic capital of the classical world — burning much of the lower city and the old marketplace, a destruction archaeologists can still see in the ground today.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The raiders at Athens were primarily the Heruli (a Germanic group allied with the Goths), not Goths themselves — the sources distinguish them, though both groups operated together in this era's Aegean raids. Before the attack, Athens was recently walled, yet the defenses failed; afterward, the Athenian historian Dexippus reportedly led citizens in driving the raiders out, one of the rare cases where a city's inhabitants fought back. Athens shrank dramatically after 267, its population contracting to the area around the Roman Agora, enclosed by a new hasty wall.

events.label: Raid on Ephesus and Asia Minor
events.description: Gothic and allied raiders struck Ephesus (in modern western Turkey), one of the wealthiest cities in the Roman world, looting the famous Temple of Artemis — one of the Seven Wonders of the ancient world — in the 260s CE.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The Temple of Artemis at Ephesus had already been burned once before, by a lone arsonist named Herostratus in 356 BCE (the night Alexander the Great was born, ancient writers loved to note). The Gothic raid was the temple's final serious blow; it was never fully restored to its former glory afterward, eventually falling into ruin and disuse as Christianity spread through the region.

events.label: Battle of Naissus
events.description: Around 269 CE, Emperor Claudius II shattered a massive Gothic host at Naissus (modern Niš, Serbia), then spent months hunting down survivors through the Balkan mountains, ending the great Gothic raiding era in a grinding campaign rather than a single decisive stroke.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The victory at Naissus was not just one battle: disease ripped through the crowded Gothic camps during and after the fighting, finishing what the Roman cavalry had started. The battle's exact year is disputed — sources give 268 or 269 CE — and some evidence suggests the future emperor Aurelian played a key role leading the cavalry pursuit that turned a battle win into a near-total destruction.

events.label: Claudius II 'Gothicus'
events.description: After Naissus, the Senate awarded Emperor Claudius II the victory title 'Gothicus' (conqueror of the Goths) — then he died of plague the following year and was deified, becoming one of Rome's most honored short-reign emperors.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Claudius Gothicus reigned only about two years (268–270 CE), yet the Senate declared him a god and later emperors, including Constantine, claimed him as an ancestor to borrow his prestige. Many of the Goths his army didn't kill were settled inside the empire as coloni — tied tenant farmers — on Balkan land emptied by years of raiding and plague, a policy that foreshadowed how Rome would eventually absorb (and be transformed by) the very peoples it fought.

events.label: Aurelian Abandons Dacia
events.description: In 271 CE, Emperor Aurelian made a blunt strategic decision: he pulled the Roman army and administration out of Dacia (roughly modern Transylvania), abandoned a province Rome had held for 165 years, and shortened the Danube frontier to something he could actually defend.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Aurelian called the abandoned territory 'Dacia Aureliana' — renaming it on the safe side of the Danube as if the label could soften the loss. Despite giving up Dacia, Aurelian went on to reunify the entire fractured empire (it had briefly split into three competing pieces) and earned the title Restitutor Orbis, 'Restorer of the World.' The Roman population he evacuated from old Dacia left behind towns, farms, and a century and a half of Roman graves — a ghost province.

events.label: Visigoths and Ostrogoths Diverge
events.description: By around 290 CE the Gothic world had fractured into two distinct peoples divided by the Dniester River: the Tervingi to the west (ancestors of the Visigoths) and the Greuthungi to the east (ancestors of the Ostrogoths), with the familiar 'Visigoth/Ostrogoth' labels only solidifying centuries later.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The tidy 'western Goths/eastern Goths' translation is almost certainly wrong — 'Visigoth' likely meant something closer to 'noble Goths' and 'Ostrogoth' something like 'Goths of the rising sun,' honorific labels rather than compass directions. The neat two-tribe scheme was largely popularized by the sixth-century writer Jordanes, working for an Ostrogothic court that wanted a clean, ancient pedigree — making it partly a retrojection onto a messier reality of many shifting groups.

events.label: The Tervingi Reiks System
events.description: The Tervingi governed themselves through a council of noble warriors called reiks (a Gothic word related to the Latin rex) who could elevate a single war-leader in times of crisis — but never a hereditary king, because their system was built on consent, not blood.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Roman sources deliberately called the Tervingi's paramount leader a 'judge,' not a king — a word choice that signals bounded authority through arbitration rather than rulership by right. The reiks title is related to the root that survives in the modern German word 'Reich' (realm/empire), showing how deeply this political vocabulary embedded itself in later European history.

events.label: Greuthungi Royal Lineage
events.description: Out on the open steppe east of the Dniester, the Greuthungi took a different political path from their Tervingi cousins: they developed a centralized hereditary kingship anchored in a single royal house, the Amali dynasty, who bolstered their rule with a pedigree of heroic and semi-divine ancestors.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The Amali dynasty's elaborate founding genealogy — tracing their lineage back through heroes and demigods — was recorded by the sixth-century historian Jordanes, who was writing for an Ostrogothic court that commissioned the history, making the deep ancestral generations essentially dynastic propaganda. That same Amali line eventually produced Theodoric the Great, the Gothic king who ruled Italy from a marble palace in Ravenna.

events.label: The Gothic Black Sea Trade
events.description: Positioned on the Pontic steppe north of the Black Sea, the Goths sat astride the exchange routes between the Roman Empire and the barbarian interior — controlling the flow of grain, slaves, furs, and Roman prestige goods that made Gothic war-leaders rich.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The Black Sea coast had been ringed with Greek colonial cities for a thousand years before the Goths arrived, and those cities were now under Roman influence, full of merchants and grain ships. The Goths effectively became the middlemen between those coastal trading ports and the vast steppe interior. The same prestige-goods mechanism that had enriched chiefs in earlier Germanic societies ran at full strength here, but on a much larger scale — the Black Sea was one of the most commercially active bodies of water in the ancient world.

events.label: Gothic Social Tiers: Nobles, Freemen, Slaves
events.description: Gothic society in the third and fourth centuries was stratified into three layers: an aristocratic warrior class at the top, free farmers who owned land and served in war in the middle, and at the bottom a dependent and enslaved population that included Roman captives taken in the great raids.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The archaeological evidence from Chernyakhov culture sites (the village remains left by the Goths of this era) is unambiguous: this was a settled, farming people, not a nomadic camp. Roman prisoners and their descendants supplied the agricultural labor that kept the aristocracy's estates running, making the Gothic raids partly a labor-acquisition system.

events.label: Gothic Settlement Agriculture
events.description: Chernyakhov-culture sites reveal substantial, permanent villages with long timber houses, sunken-floored workshops, and grain storage facilities — the archaeological profile of a settled farming society, not a wandering horde.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The presence of granaries implies not just subsistence farming but surplus — enough stored grain to feed specialists and to trade. Iron tools found at these sites were used for field work, meaning Gothic agriculture was productive enough to require proper tooling. This picture of settled prosperity is one reason historians now argue the Goths were not simply pushed westward by the Huns out of desperation — they were a wealthy, organized society that had to be militarily defeated before it moved.

events.label: Constantine's Gothic Treaty
events.description: Emperor Constantine I concluded a treaty with the Tervingi that secured grain supplies and Gothic military recruits for the Roman army in exchange for subsidies and trade privileges.

events.label: Early Christianity Among the Goths
events.description: Christianity reached the Goths not through official missions but through Roman captives taken in the third-century raids and resettled among Gothic communities. These prisoners kept their faith, passed it to their children and their captors' neighbors, and created a small Christian presence among the Goths generations before any bishop crossed the frontier.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: This bottom-up transmission pattern — through the unfree rather than the powerful — is what made Gothic Christianity durable. Because it spread first among captives with no political leverage, it took root as a personal and community faith before it ever became a leadership decision. By the time Ulfilas arrived with an official mandate, he was building on a foundation already decades old.

events.label: Ulfilas Consecrated Bishop of the Goths
events.description: Around 341 CE, Ulfilas ("little wolf" in Gothic) traveled to Constantinople and was consecrated bishop by Eusebius of Nicomedia, receiving a formal church mandate to bring Christianity to his people across the Danube. The bishop who consecrated him was a leading Arian — a detail that permanently shaped what kind of Christians the Goths would become.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Ulfilas was of Cappadocian Greek descent (modern central Turkey), probably tracing his ancestry to Roman captives taken in the third-century Gothic raids. He served as bishop to the Goths for roughly four decades, dying around 383 CE. His Gothic name, Wulfila, survives alongside the Greek form Ulfilas in the ancient sources.

events.label: Ulfilas Translates the Gothic Bible
events.description: Around 350 CE, the Gothic bishop Ulfilas (also spelled Wulfila) invented a new alphabet specifically for the Gothic language and used it to translate the Bible — giving the Goths their own written scripture and making them the first Germanic people with a literary tradition in their own tongue.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Ulfilas was of Cappadocian Greek descent (from what is now central Turkey) and had been ordained bishop of the Goths in Constantinople around 341. His translation was Arian Christian, which is why Gothic Christianity remained Arian for generations — a doctrinal detail that would shape Gothic diplomacy and identity long after Ulfilas himself died around 383.

events.label: The Gothic Bible
events.description: The Gothic Bible is the oldest substantial text in any Germanic language — by roughly three centuries. That means the deepest written root of English, German, Dutch, and every Scandinavian language is not a Norse saga or an Anglo-Saxon poem but a fourth-century Gothic Gospel translated by an Arian bishop the Roman church had condemned.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Most of what survives is the four Gospels and parts of Paul's letters; the Old Testament text is almost entirely lost. Because Gothic was written down so early, before the Germanic family had drifted apart, the language preserves sounds and forms that linguists use to reconstruct Proto-Germanic, the unwritten common ancestor. The Beowulf manuscript is roughly six hundred years younger.

events.label: The Gothic Alphabet
events.description: To write Gothic down, Ulfilas engineered an alphabet from scratch: roughly 25–27 letters pulling most letterforms from Greek, a few from Latin, and a handful of runic shapes for sounds neither classical script could handle. It was not an evolution from earlier scripts but a purpose-built tool, designed to do one specific job.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Scholars count the letter total differently because a few characters are contested — some may be numerals borrowed into the alphabet rather than true letters. The Gothic alphabet is notable for being one of the very few writing systems in history whose inventor is actually known by name. The Greek-majority letterforms reflect Ulfilas's own bilingual Greek-Gothic background.

events.label: The Goths Adopt Arian Christianity
events.description: Arianism (named for the Alexandrian priest Arius) held that God the Son was created by the Father and subordinate to him — not co-eternal, not of the same substance. The Council of Nicaea condemned it as heresy in 325 CE, but it remained in imperial favor for decades, and when Ulfilas was consecrated, the churchman who commissioned him was firmly on the Arian side.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The Nicene Creed's phrase "of one substance with the Father" (Greek: homoousios) was specifically drafted to rule out the Arian position — the single word homoousios was the crux of the whole dispute. For much of the mid-fourth century Roman emperors backed Arian bishops, making Arianism not a fringe heresy but a court theology. When the Goths later ruled Catholic populations in Gaul, Spain, and Italy, the religious divide between Arian rulers and Nicene subjects created a fault line that helped end every Gothic kingdom.

events.label: The Nicene-Arian Divide Among Goths
events.description: The Gothic church's Arian theology put it at odds with the emerging Catholic orthodoxy, a theological split that would shape Gothic-Roman relations for two centuries.

events.label: Pagan Gothic Persecution of Christians
events.description: Around 370 CE, Athanaric launched a persecution of Gothic Christians, rolling a wagon bearing images of the old pagan gods from settlement to settlement and forcing every household to sacrifice before it. Those who refused — the Christians — were publicly identified by their refusal and killed, with one remembered incident of a congregation burned alive inside their tent-church while they sang.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The moving-idol test was a deliberate loyalty ritual that made Christian identity visible in front of an entire community — refusal was a public act, not a private one. The Gothic church produced its own named martyrs from this persecution, and a church with martyrs tends to grow rather than shrink. The persecution is the clearest evidence that Gothic Christianity was already a significant social force, not a fringe phenomenon, by the time Athanaric felt threatened enough to act.

events.label: Athanaric, Judge of the Visigoths
events.description: Athanaric held power over the Tervingi Goths in the 360s and 370s as their "judge" — a title that carried paramount authority without the hereditary weight of a king. He fought off Roman incursions, suppressed Gothic Christians as a political threat, and ended his days as a refugee welcomed into Constantinople by the emperor Theodosius, dying there in 381 CE.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: When the Huns shattered Gothic society in 375, Athanaric refused to cross the Danube into the empire, retreating instead into the Carpathians — a point of pride that soon became untenable. Theodosius gave him a state funeral in Constantinople with full imperial honors, a remarkable gesture toward a former enemy. Athanaric is sometimes called the first king of the Visigoths, though he never used that title himself.

events.label: Ermanaric's Greuthungi Empire
events.description: The Greuthungi king Ermanaric dominated a wide swath of the Pontic steppe (the grassland north of the Black Sea) in the mid-fourth century, subjugating the Heruli, Slavic peoples, and Finnic groups — and becoming so celebrated that Germanic peoples were still singing epic songs about him in the Viking Age.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Ermanaric is one of only a handful of Gothic figures mentioned in two separate Roman sources: the eyewitness historian Ammianus Marcellinus and the much later Jordanes. The legend of his death is grimly memorable: a woman of a subject people was torn apart by horses on his orders, and her brothers wounded him so badly he died slowly as the Huns closed in — a story that surfaced centuries later in both Old Norse and Old English verse.

events.label: The Codex Argenteus
events.description: The Codex Argenteus (Latin: "the silver book") is a sixth-century luxury copy of the Gothic Gospels made in Ostrogothic Italy: purple-dyed vellum, entire text in silver ink, opening lines and holy names in gold. It is the single most important surviving witness to Ulfilas's translation — a heretical barbarian scripture that became one of the great treasures of European manuscript history.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Of the original 336 leaves, 187 survive, now permanently displayed at Uppsala University's Carolina Rediviva library in Sweden, where it is known as "Silverbibeln" (the Silver Bible). It was added to UNESCO's Memory of the World Register in 2011. The manuscript was probably produced at Ravenna for the Ostrogothic court, making it as much a political statement about Gothic legitimacy as a religious text.

events.label: The Huns Shatter the Greuthungi
events.description: Around 375 CE, the Huns swept in from the eastern steppe and destroyed the Greuthungi (eastern Goths), collapsing the great domain that Ermanaric had built — and sending terrified survivors westward to warn the Tervingi that something unstoppable was coming.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The Huns had arrived on the Volga as early as 370 CE, kicking off a chain reaction that pushed Goths, Alans, Vandals, Gepids, and half a dozen other peoples out of their homelands at once. By around 430 they would consolidate a vast empire on the Danubian frontier — but in 375 they were still a shock to the system that no Roman geographer had mapped or anticipated.

events.label: Ermanaric's Death Before the Huns
events.description: Around 375 CE, Ermanaric — the Greuthungi king whose domain stretched across much of the Ukrainian steppe — died as the Hunnic assault overwhelmed his realm; ancient sources disagree on whether he fell in battle or took his own life rather than survive the destruction of everything he had built.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Ammianus Marcellinus describes Ermanaric as a 'warlike king' who commanded great areas of Scythia, while the sixth-century historian Jordanes later inflated him into a legendary conqueror to rival Alexander. In later Germanic heroic legend Ermanaric became a figure of tragic treachery, appearing in Old English poetry and Norse sagas long after the Goths themselves had vanished as a distinct people.

events.label: Hunnic Cavalry Tactics on the Steppe
events.description: The Huns fought from horseback using a composite reflex bow — a short, recurved weapon built of layered wood, horn, and sinew that packed the punch of a much longer bow and could be fired at a full gallop — a combination the Gothic infantry-and-charge model had no answer for.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The feigned retreat was central to Hunnic tactics: they would shower an enemy with arrows, ride away the instant the line advanced, then swarm back when it broke formation and tired. Gothic strength was built around a single disciplined infantry stand followed by a noble cavalry charge — both of which the Huns simply declined to receive, making Gothic military skill nearly useless against them.

events.label: Fritigern Leads the Goths Across the Danube
events.description: In 376 CE the Tervingi chieftain Fritigern led his entire people — men, women, children, the old and sick — to the north bank of the Danube and petitioned Emperor Valens to let them cross into the Roman Empire, the first time an entire Germanic nation had asked to be admitted as refugees rather than invaders.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Fritigern's decisive move was framing his people as Arian Christians, the same branch of Christianity the emperor Valens personally favored — a calculated bit of religious diplomacy that made the emperor far more sympathetic. Valens saw an upside too: a settled barbarian nation would mean new taxpayers and, crucially, a massive pool of military recruits he badly needed for wars on his eastern frontier.

events.label: Starvation and Exploitation of Gothic Refugees
events.description: The Roman officials assigned to receive and feed the Gothic refugees — Lupicinus and Maximus — treated the crisis as a money-making opportunity: they sold the starving Goths food at extortionate prices, and when the Goths ran out of money and goods, accepted Gothic children as slaves in exchange for grain, sometimes at the rate of one child per dog.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: This episode is recorded by Roman sources themselves, not by Gothic ones — meaning it is the conquerors' own confession of what happened. The Gothic War of 376–382 that followed is now considered one of the causes historians point to in the long decline of the Western Roman Empire, though scholars still debate just how decisive Adrianople really was.

events.label: Lupicinus' Treacherous Feast
events.description: In 377 CE the Roman commander Lupicinus invited Gothic leaders including Fritigern to a banquet and attempted to murder them there — a classic Roman gambit to decapitate a restless group's leadership in a single stroke. Fritigern escaped, and the full revolt across the province of Thrace erupted immediately after.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The Gothic War that followed drew in not just the Tervingi but surviving Greuthungi who had also crossed the Danube, escaped Gothic slaves, and workers from Thracian mines where sold Goths had been put to forced labor underground — a coalition of the desperate that Rome had inadvertently created. The war burned through the Balkans for two full years before Valens marched a field army to end it at Adrianople in 378.

events.label: Battle of Adrianople
events.description: On August 9, 378 CE, outside the city of Adrianople in what is now European Turkey, the Gothic leader Fritigern destroyed the eastern Roman field army and killed the reigning emperor in a single afternoon — the worst Roman defeat since Cannae in 216 BCE.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Adrianople was fought in the Roman province of Thracia, placing the catastrophe deep inside imperial territory, not at the frontier. The ancient historian Ammianus Marcellinus, who was a soldier himself, explicitly reached for Cannae as his comparison — meaning not just a bad loss but the worst category of loss that existed in Roman historical memory. The battle took barely an afternoon to end an army that could not be replaced.

events.label: Death of Emperor Valens
events.description: Emperor Valens was killed at Adrianople, becoming the first reigning Roman emperor to die at the hands of a foreign enemy in over a century — his body was never recovered, and the tradition that he burned to death anonymously in a peasant farmhouse cannot be confirmed.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Valens had come to power in 364 not through military glory but as co-emperor appointed by his elder brother Valentinian I, who handed him the eastern half of the empire to manage. His reign was largely unremarkable before Adrianople, which makes the manner of his death — the master of the Roman world vanishing into a burning barn, unrecognized — one of the more haunting images of the late Roman period.

events.label: Gothic Heavy Cavalry at Adrianople
events.description: The Gothic Greuthungi cavalry (the heavily armored lancers of the eastern Goths, inheritors of steppe riding traditions) returned from foraging at exactly the moment the Roman line was locked forward against the Gothic wagon-ring, crashed into the exposed Roman flank, and turned a hard fight into a massacre.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Gothic leader Fritigern deliberately stalled the battle with envoys and drawn-out negotiations — not out of hesitation but to buy time for his cavalry to return. The Roman infantry in the final crush were packed so tightly by the pressure from two sides that contemporary sources say men could not raise their weapons or even fall when they were killed. It was discipline and patience, not a lucky flank charge, that destroyed Rome that day.

events.label: Theodosius I Rebuilds the Eastern Army
events.description: After Adrianople shattered the eastern field army, the new emperor Theodosius I spent years recruiting massively to rebuild it — including recruiting Goths themselves — accelerating the long trend of the Roman army filling up with the very peoples it had been fighting.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Theodosius was Roman emperor from 379 to 395, handed the eastern throne specifically because the east needed a capable general after Adrianople. His rebuilding strategy was pragmatic rather than principled: he needed bodies, the Goths were formidable fighters, and the empire's earlier manpower base had been badly depleted by decades of plague and civil war. He would later be called 'the Great' partly for holding the empire together through this crisis, though the terms he made with the Goths were widely recognized even at the time as disadvantageous.

events.label: The Gothic Foedus of 382
events.description: The foedus (treaty) of 382 CE settled the Goths inside the Roman Empire as a semi-autonomous armed nation — keeping their own leaders, fighting in their own units under their own commanders, and governing themselves on collectively granted Balkan land — terms without precedent in Roman history.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The novelty was not that barbarians were settled inside the empire (that had happened under Marcus Aurelius) but that this group was never broken up or absorbed as individual recruits. Earlier settled peoples were distributed, disarmed, and Romanized; the Goths of 382 remained organized, armed, and self-governing. Theodosius's own contemporaries noted the arrangement was disadvantageous — a nominal ally that answered to Gothic commanders, not Roman ones.

events.label: The Foedus as a Constitutional Novelty
events.description: The 382 treaty ending the Gothic War was unlike any deal Rome had struck before: it settled the Goths collectively on imperial land in Moesia (modern Bulgaria), let them keep their own commanders and internal laws, and exempted them from Roman civil jurisdiction — a barbarian nation living inside the empire but not absorbed by it.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Rome had used the foederati ("treaty people") arrangement for generations with small war-bands, giving them land and provisions in exchange for military service. The 382 settlement scaled that bargain to an entire sovereign-ish people for the first time, setting a template that Visigoths, Vandals, and Burgundians would all use in the fifth century when the western empire began to dissolve around them.

events.label: Alaric Becomes King of the Visigoths
events.description: Alaric I was the first king of the Visigoths, rising to lead the Goths settled in Moesia (the Balkans territory acquired after Adrianople) in 395 CE — immediately after Theodosius's death left his people unpaid, leaderless, and freshly bled at the Frigidus.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Alaric came to leadership of the very Goths who had occupied Moesia since the post-Adrianople settlement — he was a product of the foedus system, a Gothic commander who had served in Roman forces. His subsequent career was not simple warlordism but a prolonged, often frustrated attempt to get the empire to give his people the pay and formal status they had been promised and never fully received. The sack of Rome in 410 was the end of that negotiation failing.

events.label: Death of Theodosius I and Empire's Division
events.description: When Theodosius I died in 395 CE, he was the last man to rule the entire Roman Empire; at his death the empire split permanently between his two young sons, east and west, and the Gothic federates inside it — unpaid, resentful after the Frigidus — chose their own king and began to move.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Theodosius left the west to his son Honorius (age 10) and the east to Arcadius (age 17), neither capable of managing the Gothic problem their father had barely contained by force of personal authority. The split at his death was not formally declared permanent — no one announced the end of a united empire — but the two courts never reunited, and the division hardened immediately into a structural reality that no later emperor could reverse.

events.label: Alaric Ravages Greece
events.description: Alaric led his army through Thrace and Greece, sacking Corinth, Argos, and Sparta while the western commander Stilicho maneuvered fruitlessly on the Peloponnese.

events.label: Stilicho and Alaric: Rival and Partner
events.description: The half-Vandal Roman general Stilicho was the western empire's most powerful commander for over a decade, repeatedly outfighting Alaric but never finishing him off — a deliberate choice that kept the Gothic army as a political tool.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Stilicho was married to Serena, the niece of Emperor Theodosius I, making him family to the imperial house even as rivals used his Vandal ancestry against him. He served simultaneously as guardian to the boy-emperor Honorius, meaning the defense of Rome rested almost entirely on a man who was, by the old Roman definition, a barbarian himself. His refusal to destroy Alaric outright was likely a calculated gamble: keeping a formidable Gothic army intact gave Stilicho leverage over the eastern court in Constantinople, with which he had a long territorial dispute over Illyricum.

events.label: Alaric as Master of Soldiers in Illyricum
events.description: The eastern court briefly legitimized Alaric by appointing him military governor of Illyricum, a title that gave his army legal status and access to imperial arms factories.

events.label: Alaric's First Invasion of Italy
events.description: Alaric invaded Italy, besieging Milan and forcing the imperial court to flee to the more defensible city of Ravenna, where it would remain for decades.

events.label: Battle of Pollentia
events.description: On Easter Sunday 402, Stilicho launched a surprise attack on Alaric's army at Pollentia in northern Italy, capturing the Gothic baggage train — the wagons carrying families, supplies, and plunder — and forcing Alaric to retreat from Italy.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The timing was deliberate and controversial: attacking on the holiest day of the Christian calendar was seen by many as a scandal, and the Gothic troops, many of whom were also Christians, were initially caught off-guard by the violation of the sacred truce. Despite the Roman tactical victory, Alaric was able to recover enough to fight again the following year at Verona, where Stilicho defeated him a second time but again let him escape. Alaric did not return to Italy for six years — until Stilicho was dead.

events.label: Stilicho Executed
events.description: In August 408, Emperor Honorius had his most capable general, Stilicho, arrested and beheaded on a charge of treason — one of the most self-destructive decisions in Roman history, coming just as Alaric was preparing his first march on Rome.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The purge went far beyond Stilicho himself: soldiers loyal to him were massacred across the western empire, and Roman troops then slaughtered the wives and children of the barbarian federate soldiers serving in the Roman army. The result was that tens of thousands of those federates — men who had been fighting for Rome — defected directly to Alaric, transforming his army almost overnight. Honorius then retreated to Ravenna, a city surrounded by marshes on the Adriatic coast, making it nearly impossible for Alaric to reach him and giving the emperor a safe perch from which to refuse every negotiation.

events.label: Alaric Blockades Rome
events.description: Before the famous sack, Alaric besieged Rome twice (408 and 409), each time cutting off the grain supply until the city agreed to pay enormous ransoms — his goal throughout was a negotiated settlement, not destruction.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The ransom extracted in 408, recorded by the historian Zosimus, included gold, silver, silk, dyed hides, and three thousand pounds of pepper — pepper being an Indian spice so valuable in the ancient world that it was stored like bullion. Even starving and under siege, Rome could still produce a king's ransom in luxury goods that had traveled from halfway around the world. In 409, Alaric escalated by installing a puppet emperor of his own, the city prefect Priscus Attalus, to put additional political pressure on Honorius — but the court in Ravenna still refused to grant Alaric what he actually wanted: land and a senior military title.

events.label: Alaric Sacks Rome
events.description: On August 24, 410 CE, after years of failed negotiation, the Visigoths entered Rome and plundered the city for three days — the first foreign enemy to take Rome in nearly 800 years, sending a shockwave across the entire ancient world.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The sack was notably restrained by ancient standards: Alaric, an Arian Christian, ordered the great basilicas of Saint Peter and Saint Paul treated as sanctuaries, and there was no general massacre. Jerome, translating scripture in Bethlehem when the news arrived, wrote that it struck him speechless: "the city which had taken the whole world was itself taken." Administratively, Rome was no longer even the western capital at that point — Ravenna had been the seat of government since 402 — but the symbolic force of the eternal city falling was so overwhelming that the practical fact barely registered.

events.label: Augustine Writes The City of God
events.description: After the sack, the North African bishop Augustine of Hippo began writing The City of God, a massive work refuting pagan claims that Rome fell because it abandoned its old gods — and in doing so, built the political theology that shaped medieval Europe for a thousand years.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Augustine took thirteen years to complete the work (413–426 CE), producing twenty-two books in total. Its central argument — that no earthly empire, not even Rome, was ever truly eternal, and that Christians owe their deepest loyalty to the heavenly City of God rather than any human state — gave the medieval church a philosophical basis for asserting authority independent of (and in some readings above) secular rulers. The book directly addresses questions still debated today: the existence of evil, free will versus divine foreknowledge, and the nature of just war.

events.label: Death of Alaric at Cosentia
events.description: Months after sacking Rome, Alaric died of fever somewhere in southern Italy while leading his people toward Africa — having achieved the most famous military feat of his age and gotten nothing he had actually asked for: land, a title, a home.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Alaric had spent his entire adult life inside the Roman system, fighting Rome's wars and then fighting Rome itself, all in pursuit of a formal, recognized settlement. The cruel irony is that what he wanted was modest — a senior generalship and farmland for his people — and the empire spent fifteen years refusing him things it routinely granted to other federate leaders. He was likely in his mid-forties when he died, and the cause ("fever") is vague enough that it could have been malaria, typhoid, or something else entirely; the sources are not specific.

events.label: The Busento River Burial Legend
events.description: According to Jordanes, Alaric's followers diverted the River Busento, buried him with treasure in the dry riverbed, restored the flow, and killed all the workers to keep the location secret — a story almost certainly too perfect to be literally true.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The tale comes from Jordanes, the 6th-century Gothic historian whose reliability is always in question (he was writing 150 years after the event and had clear reasons to mythologize Gothic leaders). No grave has ever been found despite periodic archaeological searches near modern Cosenza in Calabria, Italy. The story's structure — secret burial, silenced witnesses, lost treasure — mirrors other famous burial legends from the ancient world and the Migration Age, which is itself a reason to hold it lightly. What it reliably shows is how electric Alaric's death was: it generated legend almost immediately.

events.label: Athaulf Leads Visigoths into Gaul
events.description: Alaric's brother-in-law Athaulf took command of the Visigoths after 410 and led them out of Italy into southern Gaul (modern France), articulating a strikingly new idea: that Gothic arms should restore Rome, not replace it.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Athaulf's famous remark — that he had once dreamed of a Gothic empire where Rome had been, but concluded the Goths could never function without Roman law and order — survives in the historian Orosius and is one of the most remarkable self-assessments from the entire Migration Age. It suggests a Gothic leadership class that had internalized Roman governance deeply enough to recognize they could not simply discard it. Athaulf was assassinated in Barcelona in 415, barely three years into his reign, before he could fully build the state he envisioned — but the kingdom his successors built in Toulouse became exactly what he described.

events.label: Galla Placidia Marries Athaulf
events.description: At Narbonne in 414, Galla Placidia — sister of Emperor Honorius, captured in the sack of Rome — married the Gothic king Athaulf in a full Roman ceremony, a living symbol of the fused Gothic-Roman world that was being born.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Galla Placidia wore Roman robes at the wedding and the ceremony followed Roman customs, signaling Athaulf's deliberate positioning as a Roman partner, not a conqueror. She and Athaulf had a son, Theodosius, who died in infancy — his death, commemorated with a silver coffin in Barcelona, was mourned as a genuine dynastic tragedy. After Athaulf's assassination in 415, Galla Placidia was passed between Gothic factions and eventually returned to Ravenna, where she later became regent for her son Valentinian III and was one of the most powerful figures in the western empire for decades.

events.label: The Visigoths Settle in Aquitaine
events.description: In 418 CE Rome formally granted the Visigoths land in Aquitaine, the fertile southwestern Gaul region around the Garonne valley — the moment a wandering people finally got a permanent address inside the empire.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The Visigoths were settled under King Wallia, who had negotiated the deal with the imperial government; Wallia himself died the same year the settlement was formalized. The kingdom they built in Aquitaine would eventually extend far beyond Gaul to cover most of the Iberian Peninsula. Unlike the eastern empire, the Visigothic Kingdom successfully resisted Byzantine attempts to reassert Roman authority over its territory.

events.label: Kingdom of Toulouse Founded
events.description: The settlement in Aquitaine became the Kingdom of Toulouse — the first Germanic successor state to plant itself inside the western Roman world and actually make it stick, with Toulouse as the capital and Gothic king ruling over a Roman administrative apparatus.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The kingdom lasted nearly a century before its destruction at Vouillé in 507. The Visigoths maintained independence from the Eastern Roman (Byzantine) Empire even as the western half collapsed around them. Their kingdom was distinctive in keeping the Roman landowning class largely intact rather than displacing it wholesale.

events.label: Gothic Hospitalitas Land Distribution
events.description: The Visigoths were settled in Aquitaine through a Roman legal mechanism called hospitalitas — rules originally designed to billet soldiers with civilian landowners — adapted so Gothic warriors became armed neighbors to Roman estate-owners rather than conquerors.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Scholars still actively debate whether what actually changed hands under Gothic hospitalitas was the land itself or just the tax revenue from it — the sources are genuinely ambiguous. The system created a Gothic-Roman mixed society almost by design: the same legal roof covered both peoples, neither simply erasing the other.

events.label: Visigothic Church Building in Gaul
events.description: Visigothic aristocrats patronized church construction in Aquitaine, adopting Roman architectural forms and blending Arian liturgical needs with local building traditions.

events.label: Theodoric I Rules the Visigoths
events.description: Theodoric I ruled the Visigoths from 418 to 451 — a reign of over three decades that transformed the Aquitaine settlement from a Roman grant into a genuine independent power with a real capital, a real army, and a king who died in battle against the Huns.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Theodoric I was the son of Alaric's successor Ataulf's rival, and his long reign gave the kingdom rare stability in a period of violent succession. His son Thorismund was acclaimed king on the battlefield itself, surrounded by the dead of the Catalaunian Plains — one of the more dramatic royal inaugurations in Gothic history.

events.label: Visigothic Alliance with Aetius
events.description: The Roman general Aetius cultivated the Visigothic kingdom as a counterweight to other barbarian powers, using Gothic troops in his pan-Gallic defensive system.

events.label: Visigoths Fight Attila at the Catalaunian Plains
events.description: In 451 CE the Visigothic king Theodoric I died fighting alongside the Roman general Aetius to stop Attila the Hun at the Battle of the Catalaunian Plains — the largest battle of the age, fought between two coalitions that were both mostly barbarian.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The battle took place on 20 June 451 and is considered one of the last major military operations of the Western Roman Empire. Attila died only two years later in 453, and his empire rapidly disintegrated after the subsequent Battle of Nedao in 454. Historians agree the decisive moment was actually the earlier siege of Aurelianum (modern Orléans), which blocked the Hunnic advance before the plains battle even began.

events.label: Thorismund Succeeds Theodoric I
events.description: Theodoric I's son Thorismund was acclaimed king on the battlefield of the Catalaunian Plains before Aetius maneuvered him into withdrawing to Toulouse to secure his throne.

events.label: Theodoric II and Roman Collaboration
events.description: Theodoric II, who murdered his brother Thorismund to take power, cultivated close ties with Roman aristocrats and the imperial court, acting as a kingmaker in western imperial politics.

events.label: Euric Becomes Visigothic King
events.description: Euric seized the Visigothic throne in 466 by killing his brother Theodoric II, then transformed the kingdom from a nominal Roman client into an outright independent power — and expanded it dramatically across southern Gaul and most of Hispania.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Euric was the son of Theodoric I, making the family tree a sequence of murders: Thorismund killed (by Theodoric II), Theodoric II killed (by Euric). He ruled until 484, one of the longer Gothic reigns. His expansion happened to coincide exactly with the final collapse of the western empire in the 470s, which left a power vacuum he was well-positioned to fill.

events.label: The Code of Euric
events.description: Around 475 Euric issued the Code of Euric — one of the earliest written law codes produced by any Germanic people, blending Gothic custom with Roman legal form, drafted in Latin by a Roman lawyer named Leo.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The man who actually compiled the code was Leo of Narbonne, a Roman lawyer and Euric's principal counsellor — meaning a Roman jurist wrote the legal foundation of a Gothic kingdom. The code was issued probably at Toulouse and confirmed Gothic customs while reshaping them in Roman legal language. It would later be superseded, partly, by Alaric II's Breviary, which was aimed specifically at the Roman subjects Euric's code had largely ignored.

events.label: Euric Conquers Most of Hispania
events.description: In the 470s Euric's armies swept across the Iberian Peninsula, ending the last remnants of direct Roman administration and making the Visigoths the dominant power in the western Mediterranean — all while the western empire was visibly dying around him.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Euric's Iberian conquests came during the same window (around 476) when Romulus Augustulus, the last western Roman emperor, was deposed by Odoacer — meaning Euric effectively outlasted the empire he was supposedly serving. He ruled until 484, leaving his son Alaric II a kingdom spanning most of the Iberian Peninsula plus large parts of southern Gaul.

events.label: Odoacer Deposes the Last Western Emperor
events.description: In 476 CE a Germanic officer named Odoacer ("OH-doh-AY-ser") deposed the last western emperor — a child named Romulus Augustulus — sent the imperial regalia to Constantinople, and ruled Italy as king himself, the act historians traditionally call the fall of the Western Roman Empire.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Odoacer was from the Middle Danube region and had risen through the ranks of the Roman army before leading the revolt. He kept the Roman Senate functioning and the civil administration almost entirely intact during his 17-year rule, meaning Theodoric inherited a working state, not a ruin. The eastern emperor formally recognized him only as a kind of viceroy, never fully endorsing his title.

events.label: Odoacer and the Roman Senate
events.description: Odoacer nominally acknowledged eastern imperial sovereignty while ruling Italy independently, maintaining the Roman Senate and administrative apparatus with largely Roman personnel.

events.label: Gothic Polychrome Metalwork
events.description: Gothic smiths perfected garnet cloisonné goldwork, an elite craft technique that spread across the migrating Germanic world.

events.label: Breviary of Alaric
events.description: In 506 CE Alaric II published the Breviary of Alaric — a full digest of Roman law, compiled by Roman jurists, officially issued for his Gallo-Roman subjects — a barbarian king producing an authoritative edition of Roman law for the Romans he ruled.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The Breviary was promulgated on 2 February 506, the 22nd year of Alaric II's reign. It explicitly did not apply to Visigothic nobles, who continued to live under Euric's Gothic code — the two populations had separate legal systems running in parallel under one king. The text also addressed Catholic Church matters in Book 16, even though Alaric himself was Arian.

events.label: Battle of Vouillé
events.description: At the Battle of Vouillé in 507 CE, Clovis and his Frankish army crushed the Visigoths and killed Alaric II, ending the Kingdom of Toulouse and driving the surviving Visigoths south across the Pyrenees into Spain.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Clovis had converted to Catholic Christianity around 500 CE, which allowed him to frame the war against the Arian Visigoths as a holy cause — and the Catholic Gallo-Roman population of the Gothic kingdom had little reason to resist a Catholic conqueror. The battle was fought near modern Poitiers. The later bishop Gregory of Tours recorded a tradition that Clovis killed Alaric II personally, though most historians treat the personal duel as legendary embellishment.

events.label: Frankish-Visigothic Rivalry
events.description: The Catholic Frankish king Clovis framed his campaign against the Arian Visigoths as a holy war, exploiting the religious divide between Gothic rulers and their Gallo-Roman Catholic subjects.

events.label: Visigoths Retain Septimania
events.description: After Vouillé the Visigoths held onto the strip of Mediterranean coast around Narbonne (Septimania), their last foothold north of the Pyrenees, under Ostrogothic protection.

events.label: The Visigothic Kingdom of Toledo
events.description: After the loss of Gaul, the Visigoths rebuilt their kingdom on the Iberian Peninsula with Toledo as its new capital — a state that would rule most of Spain for two more centuries after the western empire itself was gone.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The Visigothic Kingdom of Toledo eventually resolved its Arian-Catholic divide by converting the whole Gothic people to Catholic Christianity — the same fault line that had helped destroy the Toulouse kingdom was finally closed. The kingdom lasted until 711, when an Arab and Berber army crossed from North Africa and destroyed it, ending over 300 years of Gothic rule on the peninsula.

events.label: Theodoric Sent West by Constantinople
events.description: Around 488, Emperor Zeno of Constantinople solved his Theodoric problem with elegant cynicism: he commissioned the restless Ostrogothic king to invade Italy and overthrow Odoacer, dispatching one dangerous force by aiming it at another.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Theodoric had spent years as a hostage in Constantinople as a boy, absorbing Roman imperial culture firsthand. Despite only ever calling himself rex (king), later Italian aristocrats gave him the imperial title princeps, and Constantinople sent him the actual western imperial regalia in 497. His realm eventually stretched from the Atlantic to the Adriatic, making him the most powerful ruler in the former western empire.

events.label: Theodoric Defeats Odoacer at Isonzo and Verona
events.description: In 489 Theodoric crushed Odoacer in two major pitched battles — at the Isonzo River near the Alps and then again near Verona — driving him back toward Ravenna and establishing Gothic supremacy in the Italian field.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: A third battle followed at the Adda River in 490 before Odoacer was finally pinned inside Ravenna. The speed of the Gothic advance surprised contemporary observers; within a single campaign season Theodoric had seized most of the peninsula, leaving only the swamp-fortified capital to reduce. Theodoric fought at the head of an entire migrating people, not just an army.

events.label: Siege of Ravenna
events.description: After sweeping the Italian field, Theodoric found Ravenna effectively impregnable: the city sat in marshland that made assault impossible, and he had to blockade it for three years before starvation and a Gothic naval victory forced Odoacer to negotiate.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Ravenna had been the western imperial capital since 402 because its swamp-girdle made it nearly impossible to take by force — the same quality that would keep it as Theodoric's own capital afterward. The naval battle that broke the siege cut off Odoacer's last supply route across the Adriatic. The city yielded in 493 by treaty, not by storm.

events.label: Theodoric the Great Conquers Italy
events.description: In 493 Theodoric the Great founded the Ostrogothic Kingdom of Italy, ruling as king from Ravenna and deliberately presenting himself as a restorer of Roman civilization rather than its conqueror.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Theodoric was the first ruler since the empire's fracture to hold a domain stretching from what is now southern France to the western Balkans. He governed as a patrician of the eastern empire in theory while acting as a fully independent western king in practice — a studied legal ambiguity that kept Constantinople nominally satisfied. The Italian Senate, the consulship, and the Roman tax system all continued under his rule with minimal disruption.

events.label: Theodoric Kills Odoacer at Ravenna
events.description: Ten days after the peace treaty that was supposed to give both men joint rule of Italy, Theodoric personally killed Odoacer at a banquet — a founding act of treachery that the later philosopher-king's admirers never satisfactorily explained away.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The later writer Jordanes recorded a grim warrior's quip attributed to Theodoric on surveying the body: that Odoacer "had no bones in him," meaning the sword had passed clean through. Historians treat the anecdote as almost certainly invented by a court-flattering source, though the murder itself is not in doubt. Odoacer had ruled Italy for 17 years and by most accounts done so reasonably well.

events.label: Theodoric's Ravenna
events.description: Theodoric adorned his capital with churches and his own monumental mausoleum, fusing Gothic power with Roman splendor.

events.label: Sant'Apollinare Nuovo, Ravenna
events.description: In 504 Theodoric dedicated Sant'Apollinare Nuovo in Ravenna, his personal palace chapel, and lined its walls with mosaics of exceptional quality — an Arian church built to proclaim that Gothic Christianity was every bit as magnificent as Roman Catholicism.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The basilica was originally dedicated to "Christ the Redeemer"; its current name dates only from the 9th century, after Catholic authorities took it over and systematically replaced the Arian mosaics with their own. Some of Theodoric's original mosaics survive in the upper nave, including a famous procession of martyrs — though the portraits of Gothic courtiers that once flanked the palace mosaic were scraped out after the Byzantine conquest. The building is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

events.label: Mausoleum of Theodoric Built
events.description: Around 520 Theodoric built his own mausoleum outside Ravenna, crowned with a single monolithic limestone slab roughly 33 feet (10 meters) across and weighing around 230 tons — a dome that is one solid piece of rock, not Roman mortared masonry.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The leading theory is that the stone was quarried on the Istrian coast across the Adriatic, though a closer Apennine source is also argued; how it was moved and lifted without modern equipment remains unexplained. The building is the only Ostrogothic royal monument still standing in anything close to its original form. After the Byzantine conquest Theodoric's bones were reportedly removed and the tomb repurposed, but the structure itself survived intact.

events.label: Ostrogothic Dual Administration
events.description: Theodoric ran Italy as a deliberate dual state: Goths held all military posts, Romans ran every civil office — the Senate, courts, treasury, and bureaucracy — creating a kingdom that looked Roman from the inside and Gothic from the barracks.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Theodoric formally called himself "King of the Goths and Romans," signaling that he intended to govern both peoples rather than just rule over one. The old senatorial dynasties like the Anicii and Symmachi found the Gothic regime a stable patron; their consuls and prefects served as under Theodoric much as under any Roman emperor. The Ostrogothic Kingdom at its peak encompassed most of Italy and significant parts of the western Balkans and southern France.

events.label: Edictum Theodorici
events.description: Theodoric issued the Edictum Theodorici, a law code applying equally to Goths and Romans, intended to reduce friction between the two communities sharing the same peninsula under very different legal traditions.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The Edictum is one of several Germanic law codes from this era (alongside Visigothic and Burgundian codes) that tried to manage the collision of Roman civil law and Germanic customary law in the same territory. Its date is still debated by scholars — some place it early in the reign, others later. The code's very existence shows Theodoric understood that a dual military-civil state only works if the two sides have a common legal floor to stand on.

events.label: Roman Aristocrats in Theodoric's Court
events.description: Leading Roman families — including the Anicii and Symmachi — served as consuls and prefects under Theodoric, finding the Ostrogothic regime a reasonably stable patron of traditional Roman culture.

events.label: Cassiodorus Serves the Gothic Court
events.description: The Roman senator Cassiodorus ("kas-ee-oh-DOR-us") served as Theodoric's chief administrator and letter-writer, producing the official correspondence that kept the Gothic-Roman dual state running, and later founded a monastery dedicated to preserving classical learning.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Cassiodorus's collected letters (the Variae) are one of the primary sources for Theodoric's reign; "Senator" was part of his family surname, not a rank. In later life he founded the Vivarium monastery in Calabria, where he organized a scriptorium to copy and preserve both Christian and classical texts at a moment when the ability to read Greek was dying in the Latin West. He also wrote a Gothic history that only survives through Jordanes's abridgment.

events.label: Cassiodorus' Variae
events.description: Cassiodorus collected his official letters and edicts from the Ostrogothic chancellery into the Variae, an indispensable source for Gothic-Roman administration and the ideals of civilized rule.

events.label: Cassiodorus Founds the Vivarium
events.description: In retirement, Cassiodorus founded the Vivarium monastery in Calabria, dedicating it to copying and preserving classical manuscripts — transmitting ancient learning through the chaos of the Gothic War's aftermath.

events.label: Boethius Executed by Theodoric
events.description: Around 523 Theodoric arrested Boethius ("boh-EE-thee-us"), the finest Roman scholar at his court, on charges of treasonous correspondence with Constantinople, and executed him in 524 without the full legal hearing his senatorial rank should have guaranteed.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Boethius had already translated portions of Aristotle's logic and written foundational textbooks on arithmetic and music before his arrest; his larger ambition was to render all of Plato and Aristotle into Latin. His local cult in the Diocese of Pavia was formally sanctioned by Rome in 1883. Theodoric also executed Boethius's father-in-law Symmachus, a respected senior senator, on related charges — a double blow that permanently damaged the Gothic regime's reputation with the Roman aristocracy.

events.label: Consolation of Philosophy
events.description: In prison awaiting execution, Boethius wrote The Consolation of Philosophy — a dialogue in which Lady Philosophy visits his cell and argues him through despair — and it became one of the most copied and translated books of the entire Middle Ages.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: The Consolation was written in 523 and is often called the last great work of the classical Western tradition. It was translated into Old English by King Alfred the Great, into Middle English by Geoffrey Chaucer, and into numerous other medieval vernaculars — its readership was wider than almost any other text between Augustine and Dante. Strikingly, the book barely mentions Christianity despite Boethius being a Christian theologian; it reasons entirely from classical Platonic and Stoic philosophy.

events.label: Execution of Senator Symmachus
events.description: Theodoric also executed Boethius' father-in-law, the respected senator Symmachus, on treason charges — acts that badly damaged the Ostrogothic regime's reputation among Roman aristocrats.

events.label: Pope John I's Mission to Constantinople
events.description: Theodoric sent Pope John I to Constantinople to negotiate the status of eastern Arians; the mission failed, and on John's return Theodoric imprisoned him, where he died.

events.label: Death of Theodoric the Great
events.description: Theodoric died leaving the kingdom to his young grandson Athalaric under his mother Amalasuntha as regent, opening an era of instability the Eastern Empire would exploit.

events.label: Amalasuntha as Regent
events.description: After Theodoric's death in 526, his daughter Amalasuntha ("ah-mah-lah-SOON-tah") ruled the Ostrogothic kingdom as regent for her young son, pushing a pro-Roman, pro-Constantinople line until Gothic nobles forced her hand, her son died, and her co-ruler had her strangled in 535.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Amalasuntha was praised by both Cassiodorus and the eastern historian Procopius as unusually wise and trilingual in Latin, Greek, and Gothic. Her insistence on giving her son Athalaric a Roman literary education rather than a warrior's upbringing was the specific flashpoint that united the Gothic nobility against her. Emperor Justinian used her murder as his legal and moral pretext to launch the Gothic War, the catastrophic 20-year conflict that would destroy both the Ostrogothic kingdom and much of Italy.

events.label: Murder of Amalasuntha
events.description: The Ostrogothic queen-regent Amalasuntha, a multilingual, Roman-educated ruler who had governed Italy on behalf of her son, was deposed and strangled by her co-ruler Theodahad in 535. Emperor Justinian, who had cultivated her as a friendly contact, seized on her murder as the legal excuse he needed to invade Italy.

details.label: Explore further
details.text: Amalasuntha governed as regent for her son Athalaric and then as queen regnant after he died — a rare case of a woman ruling an independent Germanic kingdom in her own right. Procopius describes her as speaking Latin, Greek, and Gothic fluently. Her murder came just six months after she had become sole ruler, the result of Gothic nobles who resented her pro-Roman sympathies and her authority over them.

events.label: Ostrogothic Arian Church Organization
events.description: The Ostrogoths maintained a separate Arian ecclesiastical hierarchy alongside the Catholic church, with Gothic bishops serving Gothic soldiers and nobles while Roman clergy served the Roman population.

events.label: Justinian Launches the Gothic War
events.description: In 535 Emperor Justinian I launched his great project of reconquest, sending armies to retake Italy from the Ostrogoths as part of a broader campaign to restore the old Roman Empire from Constantinople. The war would grind on for twenty years and leave Italy more ruined than any barbarian invasion had.

details.label: Explore further
